claim: Hotspot mutations of Ras drive cell transformation and tumorigenesis.
source: Hotspot mutations of Ras drive cell transformation and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Ras mutations in cancer.

claim: Several cancer-associated mutations in the switch III region moderately increase Ras activity in all isoforms.
source: Here, we show that several cancer-associated mutations in the switch III region moderately increase Ras activity in all isoforms.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Switch III mutants are biochemically inconspicuous.
source: Mutants are biochemically inconspicuous, while their clustering into nanoscale signaling complexes on the plasma membrane, termed nanocluster, is augmented.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no changes in basic biochemical parameters like GAP sensitivity and RBD binding in solution.

claim: Nanoclustering of switch III mutants is augmented.
source: Mutants are biochemically inconspicuous, while their clustering into nanoscale signaling complexes on the plasma membrane, termed nanocluster, is augmented.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and FRET-based nanoclustering data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nanoclustering dictates downstream effector recruitment.
source: Nanoclustering dictates downstream effector recruitment, MAPK-activity, and tumorigenic cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data showing correlation between nanoclustering and effector recruitment.

claim: Nanoclustering dictates MAPK-activity.
source: Nanoclustering dictates downstream effector recruitment, MAPK-activity, and tumorigenic cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased phosphorylation of MAPK pathway components.

claim: Nanoclustering dictates tumorigenic cell proliferation.
source: Nanoclustering dictates downstream effector recruitment, MAPK-activity, and tumorigenic cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation, transformation, and soft agar assays showing increased tumorigenic potential.

claim: The mechanism of signaling protein activation by nanocluster augmentation is unprecedented in cancer.
source: Our results describe an unprecedented mechanism of signaling protein activation in cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the novel findings presented in the study.

claim: Ras is dynamically anchored to cellular membranes.
source: The small GTPase Ras is dynamically anchored to cellular membranes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Ras localization.

claim: The principal steady-state localization of Ras is the plasma membrane.
source: Its principal steady-state localization is the plasma membrane, from where most of Ras signaling emerges (Hancock., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Most of Ras signaling emerges from the plasma membrane.
source: Its principal steady-state localization is the plasma membrane, from where most of Ras signaling emerges (Hancock., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ras hyperactivation is a hallmark of cancer.
source: Ras hyperactivation is a hallmark of cancer and has long been considered to be pharmacologically intractable (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology supported by citation.

claim: Ras has long been considered to be pharmacologically intractable.
source: Ras hyperactivation is a hallmark of cancer and has long been considered to be pharmacologically intractable (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recent progress encourages the pursuit of specific Ras protein inhibitors.
source: However, recent progress encourages the pursuit of specific Ras protein inhibitors (Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Hot-spot mutations in codons 12, 13, and 61 primarily compromise GAP-dependent hydrolase activity of Ras.
source: Since the seminal publication of Scheffzeck et al., it is well understood that hot-spot mutations in codons 12, 13, and 61 (Scheffzek et al., 1997), which account for >99% of Ras mutations (Prior et al., 2012), primarily compromise its GAP-dependent hydrolase activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hot-spot mutations in codons 12, 13, and 61 account for >99% of Ras mutations.
source: Since the seminal publication of Scheffzeck et al., it is well understood that hot-spot mutations in codons 12, 13, and 61 (Scheffzek et al., 1997), which account for >99% of Ras mutations (Prior et al., 2012), primarily compromise its GAP-dependent hydrolase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prior et al., 2012.

claim: Hot-spot oncogenic lesions leave Ras constitutively GTP bound.
source: These oncogenic lesions render Ras transforming and tumorigenic, as they leave Ras constitutively GTP bound and therefore ready to overdrive in particular the Ras/MAPK pathway, which critically controls cell division and other oncogenic processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of hot-spot Ras mutations.

claim: The Ras/MAPK pathway critically controls cell division and other oncogenic processes.
source: These oncogenic lesions render Ras transforming and tumorigenic, as they leave Ras constitutively GTP bound and therefore ready to overdrive in particular the Ras/MAPK pathway, which critically controls cell division and other oncogenic processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAPK pathway function.

claim: RASopathies are developmental syndromes characterized by facio-cutaneous malformations, heart developmental and neurodevelopmental defects, and predisposition to certain cancers.
source: A different mutational spectrum is found in RASopathies, developmental syndromes that are characterized by facio-cutaneous malformations, heart developmental and neurodevelopmental defects, as well as a predisposition to certain cancers (Schubbert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RASopathies supported by citation.

claim: RASopathies are characterized by hyperactivation of the Ras/MAPK-signaling pathway.
source: These syndromes are also characterized by a hyperactivation of the Ras/MAPK-signaling pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RASopathies.

claim: In Noonan syndrome, NRAS or KRAS can be mutated at various positions along their coding sequences in the germline.
source: For example, in Noonan syndrome, NRAS or KRAS can be mutated at various positions along their coding sequences in the germline.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Noonan syndrome.

claim: The exact molecular and cellular mechanisms that lead to RASopathy phenotypes are still largely unclear.
source: The exact molecular and cellular mechanisms that lead to the observed phenotypes are still largely unclear (Prior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: 20–50% of Ras proteins are organized into isoform-specific, dynamic proteo-lipid complexes that contain 6–8 Ras proteins, termed nanocluster.
source: Ras activity emerges in the plasma membrane, where 20–50% of Ras proteins are organized into isoform-specific, dynamic proteo-lipid complexes that contain 6–8 Ras proteins, termed nanocluster (Abankwa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The tight packing of Ras in nanoclusters increases its local concentration and enables more efficient effector recruitment.
source: The tight packing of this signaling protein increases its concentration locally and thus enables more efficient effector recruitment (Rotblat et al., 2010; Guzmán et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nanoclustering is a basic systems-level design principle for the generation of high-fidelity signal transduction.
source: It was proposed that nanoclustering is a basic systems-level design principle for the generation of high-fidelity signal transduction (Tian et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a proposal from prior work supported by citation.

claim: Only three regulators (galectin-1, galectin-3, and nucleophosmin) of Ras nanoclustering are known.
source: Essentially only three regulators (galectin-1 [Gal-1], galectin-3, and nucleophosmin) of Ras nanoclustering, so called nanocluster scaffolds, are known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Galectin-1 is the best characterized nanocluster scaffold.
source: The lectin Gal-1 is the best characterized nanocluster scaffold, which increases H-ras-GTP nanoclustering and effector recruitment, effectively by stabilizing immobile H-ras-GTP nanocluster (Rotblat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Galectin-1 increases H-ras-GTP nanoclustering and effector recruitment by stabilizing immobile H-ras-GTP nanocluster.
source: The lectin Gal-1 is the best characterized nanocluster scaffold, which increases H-ras-GTP nanoclustering and effector recruitment, effectively by stabilizing immobile H-ras-GTP nanocluster (Rotblat et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A novel switch III in Ras is coupled to the reorientation of H-ras on the membrane.
source: We previously revealed another aspect of Ras membrane organization, showing that a novel switch III in Ras is somehow coupled to the reorientation of H-ras on the membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors, with reference to a figure.

claim: Mutations in the switch III and structural elements of H-ras that stabilize its reorientation systematically modulate Ras signaling.
source: Mutations in the switch III and the structural elements of H-ras that stabilize its reorientation (helix α4 and the C-terminal hypervariable region [hvr]) systematically modulate Ras signaling (Gorfe et al., 2007; Abankwa et al., 2008b, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Computational modeling-derived mutations on helix α4 and the hvr alter engagement of the nanocluster modulator Gal-1 and thus H-ras nanoclustering.
source: More recently, we addressed the mechanistic basis of this activity modulation for computational modeling-derived mutations on helix α4 and the hvr: these alter engagement of the nanocluster modulator Gal-1 and thus H-ras nanoclustering.
evidence: This is a finding from recent prior work by the authors.

claim: As a consequence of altered nanoclustering, effector recruitment and subsequent downstream signaling are increased.
source: As a consequence of this up-concentration, effector recruitment and subsequent downstream signaling are increased (Guzmán et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cancer-associated mutations in the switch III region of H-, N-, and K-ras increase Ras activity by signaling protein nanocluster augmentation.
source: Here, we report that cancer-associated mutations in the switch III region of the three major Ras oncoproteins, H-, N-, and K-ras, increase Ras activity by a novel disease mechanism, namely signaling protein nanocluster augmentation.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Cancer-associated switch III mutations do not alter basic biochemical functions of Ras in solution.
source: We find that these mutations do not alter basic biochemical functions of Ras in solution.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: A strict correlation between increased recruitment of the effector to Ras and augmented nanoclustering of Ras on cellular membranes is found.
source: Instead, a strict correlation between increased recruitment of the effector to Ras and augmented nanoclustering of Ras on cellular membranes is found.
evidence: This is supported by FRET and electron microscopy data.

claim: Upregulated effector engagement is directly reflected in the elevated cellular Ras activity.
source: Upregulated effector engagement is directly reflected in the elevated cellular Ras activity, and significantly impacts on the tumorigenic potential.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and functional assays.

claim: Upregulated effector engagement significantly impacts on the tumorigenic potential.
source: Upregulated effector engagement is directly reflected in the elevated cellular Ras activity, and significantly impacts on the tumorigenic potential.
evidence: This is supported by transformation and soft agar assays.

claim: The results suggest Ras nanoclusters as direct drug targets.
source: Our results reveal a new mechanism of mutational signaling pathway hyperactivation in a pathophysiological setting and suggest Ras nanoclusters as direct drug targets.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Activating mutations D47A,E49A in the switch III region were neutralized by inactivating mutations R128A,R135A on helix α4.
source: In agreement with our model of switch III coupling to the orientation of Ras on the membrane (Abankwa et al., 2008a, 2008b), activating mutations D47A,E49A in the switch III region were neutralized by inactivating mutations R128A,R135A on helix α4, while the inactivating mutation R161A in switch III was neutralized by activating R169A,K170A in the hvr (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The inactivating mutation R161A in switch III was neutralized by activating R169A,K170A in the hvr.
source: In agreement with our model of switch III coupling to the orientation of Ras on the membrane (Abankwa et al., 2008a, 2008b), activating mutations D47A,E49A in the switch III region were neutralized by inactivating mutations R128A,R135A on helix α4, while the inactivating mutation R161A in switch III was neutralized by activating R169A,K170A in the hvr (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The neutralization results agree with an allosteric coupling of the switch III region to the reorientation of H-ras on the membrane.
source: These results therefore agree with an allosteric coupling of the switch III region to the reorientation of H-ras on the membrane.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the neutralization experiments.

claim: Mutations in the switch III could alter Ras nanoclustering by a conformation-associated mechanism.
source: Furthermore, they imply that mutations in the switch III could alter Ras nanoclustering, possibly by a conformation-associated mechanism, which we are however not going to focus on in the following, but discuss in detail at the end.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the data.

claim: H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A shows significantly increased nanoclustering compared to H-rasG12V.
source: We observed a significant increase in nanoclustering of this modeling-derived mutant, suggesting that increased signaling originates from augmented nanoclustering (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nanoclustering-FRET of H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was significantly increased at all Gal-1 levels compared to H-rasG12V.
source: As compared to H-rasG12V, nanoclustering-FRET of the modeling-derived switch III mutant H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was significantly increased at all Gal-1 levels (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: This is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A shows increased complexation with Gal-1 in cells.
source: this was also reflected by the increased complexation of this mutant with Gal-1 in the cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by Gal-1-complexation FRET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RBD-recruitment to H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was significantly increased at all Gal-1 levels compared to H-rasG12V.
source: In line with this simulation, RBD-recruitment to the structure modeling-derived switch III H-ras mutant was significantly increased at all Gal-1 levels, as compared to the parent H-rasG12V (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Raf, MEK, and ERK phosphorylation was significantly increased when H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was expressed.
source: Correspondingly, Raf, MEK, and ERK phosphorylation was significantly increased when H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was expressed, suggesting that increased nanoclustering was propagated all the way through the MAPK-signaling pathway (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Enhanced effector-recruitment of H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A was not due to an overall increase of the affinity to the Ras mutant.
source: Importantly, enhanced effector-recruitment (Figure 2E), which initiates the signal cascade was not due to an overall increase of the affinity to the Ras mutant, as revealed in anisotropy binding experiments of purified GTPγS-H-ras-D47A,E49A to the RBD in vitro (Figure 2G, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 2G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: GAP-mediated hydrolysis of H-ras-D47A,E49A was effectively unaltered compared to wt H-ras.
source: Also GAP-mediated hydrolysis (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) was effectively unaltered as compared to wt H-ras.
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: H-ras-D47A,E49A shows a relatively small decrease in the SOS-mediated GTP-analog off-rate.
source: A relatively small decrease in the SOS-mediated GTP-analog off-rate and consistently an increase in EGF-stimulated activation however suggested that this mutant may be more efficiently activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by QRET data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: H-ras-D47A,E49A shows an increase in EGF-stimulated activation.
source: A relatively small decrease in the SOS-mediated GTP-analog off-rate and consistently an increase in EGF-stimulated activation however suggested that this mutant may be more efficiently activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Increased effector recruitment and signaling of H-rasG12V-D47A,E49A is due to augmented Ras nanoclustering.
source: We conclude that increased effector recruitment (Figure 2E) and signaling (Figure 2F) of H-rasG12V with the structure modeling-derived mutation D47A,E49A in the switch III region is due to augmented Ras nanoclustering.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The computational modeling-derived switch III residues D47 and E49 are phylogenetically highly conserved.
source: The computational modeling-derived switch III residues D47 and E49 are phylogenetically highly conserved (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with a biologically significant role of their structural context.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 12% of the distinct mutations along the Ras sequences occur in the orientation-switch III regions.
source: We found that approximately 12% of the distinct mutations along the Ras sequences occur in these switch III regions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cancer genomic databases.

claim: The overall incidence of orientation-switch III mutations is very low with a total number of 15, 20, and 28 reported cases for H-, N-, and K-ras, respectively.
source: However, the overall incidence is very low with a total number of 15, 20, and 28 reported cases for H-, N-, and K-ras, respectively (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cancer genomic databases presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Orientation-switch III mutations occur most frequently in colorectal cancer samples.
source: In total, it appeared that orientation-switch III mutations occur most frequently in colorectal cancer samples.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cancer genomic databases by cancer type.

claim: The G48R mutation in H-ras is found together with a second D92N-mutation in an atypical spitzoid tumor sample.
source: In H-ras only one case of a switch III region mutation is described in an atypical spitzoid tumor (AST) sample. Curiously, this mutation G48R is found together with a second D92N-mutation in H-ras.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cancer genomic databases.

claim: The localization of H-rasG12V-G48R and H-rasG12V-G48R,D92N mutants in BHK cells was unaltered compared to parent H-rasG12V.
source: Confocal colocalization analysis confirmed that the localization of both mutants in BHK cells was unaltered as compared to parent H-rasG12V (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: H-rasG12V-G48R,D92N,R128A,R135A showed normalized H-ras activity.
source: Assuming that the G48R,D92N mutations were gain of function, we combined these cancer-associated mutations with the inactivating mutation R128A,R135A on helix α4. This new mutant showed normalized H-ras activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), comparable to the modeling-derived orientation-switch III mutants (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Electron microscopic analysis revealed a strong and significant increase in nanoclustering of H-rasG12V-G48R and H-rasG12V-G48R,D92N compared to parent H-rasG12V.
source: Indeed, electron microscopic analysis of plasma membrane sheets derived from BHK cells expressing the single or double-mutant revealed a strong and significant increase in nanoclustering of both mutants as compared to the parent H-rasG12V (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Gal-1-dose-dependent nanoclustering response was significantly increased for H-rasG12V-G48R and H-rasG12V-G48R,D92N at all Gal-1 levels.
source: This was confirmed by nanoclustering-FRET analysis in cells, where consistent with the increased Gal-1 complexation of the G48R-mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), the Gal-1-dose-dependent nanoclustering response was significantly increased for both the G48R and G48R,D92N mutants at all Gal-1 levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by nanoclustering-FRET data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Gal-1-dose-dependent RBD recruitment response of H-rasG12V-G48R and H-rasG12V-G48R,D92N was increased in cells.
source: Moreover, the Gal-1-dose-dependent RBD recruitment response of both mutants was increased in cells (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RBD-binding in vitro remained indistinguishable from the parent Ras for H-ras-G48R and H-ras-G48R,D92N.
source: while RBD-binding in vitro remained indistinguishable from the parent Ras (Figure 4E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 4E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Introduction of mutations G48R or G48R,D92N enhances effector recruitment due to increased nanoclustering.
source: Together with the absence of any RBD-binding defect, this led us to the conclusion that introduction of mutations G48R or G48R,D92N enhances effector recruitment due to increased nanoclustering.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: H-ras-G48R and H-ras-G48R,D92N remained sensitive to GAP-mediated hydrolysis.
source: As observed for the modeling-derived switch III mutant, basic biochemical parameters of H-ras-G48R or H-ras-G48R,D92N, such as GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as well as GTP affinity (Supplementary file 1) remained unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GTP affinity of H-ras-G48R and H-ras-G48R,D92N remained unaltered.
source: As observed for the modeling-derived switch III mutant, basic biochemical parameters of H-ras-G48R or H-ras-G48R,D92N, such as GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as well as GTP affinity (Supplementary file 1) remained unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Mutations G48R,D92N showed a ∼1.4-fold elevation of SOS-mediated nucleotide exchange.
source: However, mutations G48R,D92N, but not G48R alone, showed a ∼1.4-fold elevation of SOS-mediated nucleotide exchange (Supplementary file 1) consistent with an increased activation upon EGF-stimulation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: H-ras-G48R,D92N shows increased activation upon EGF-stimulation.
source: However, mutations G48R,D92N, but not G48R alone, showed a ∼1.4-fold elevation of SOS-mediated nucleotide exchange (Supplementary file 1) consistent with an increased activation upon EGF-stimulation (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In the cancer-derived H-ras mutation, a combination of weak biochemical alterations and significantly increased nanoclustering may explain the occurrence of the G48R,D92N mutations in the tumor.
source: Therefore, in this cancer-derived H-ras mutation a combination of weak biochemical alterations and a significantly increased nanoclustering, which both result in an activating phenotype of the G48R,D92N mutation in H-ras, may explain the occurrence of these two H-ras mutations in the tumor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Both N- and K-ras are more frequently mutated and associated with more aggressive cancers than H-ras.
source: For unknown reasons, both N- and K-ras are more frequently mutated and associated with more aggressive cancers than H-ras.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: N-ras is highly associated with skin and hematological cancers.
source: N-ras is highly associated with skin and hematological cancers, while K-ras is highly mutated in pancreatic and intestinal cancers (Prior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K-ras is highly mutated in pancreatic and intestinal cancers.
source: N-ras is highly associated with skin and hematological cancers, while K-ras is highly mutated in pancreatic and intestinal cancers (Prior et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The T50I mutation in N-ras was found in a malignant melanoma and is associated with Noonan syndrome.
source: In N-ras, the T50I mutation was found in a malignant melanoma and was recently also described to be associated with Noonan syndrome (Cirstea et al., 2010), a RASopathy.
evidence: This is based on cancer genomic database analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: The C51Y mutation in N-ras was found in hematologic malignancies.
source: The additional two mutations, C51Y and E49K, were found in hematologic and skin malignancies, respectively.
evidence: This is based on cancer genomic database analysis.

claim: The E49K mutation in N-ras was found in skin malignancies.
source: The additional two mutations, C51Y and E49K, were found in hematologic and skin malignancies, respectively.
evidence: This is based on cancer genomic database analysis.

claim: The highly conserved E49 is also mutated in K-ras in colorectal cancer.
source: Interestingly, the highly conserved E49 is also mutated in K-ras in colorectal cancer (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on cancer genomic database analysis presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: None of the three N-ras mutations altered the subcellular distribution of N-ras.
source: As observed for H-ras switch III mutations, none of the three N-ras mutations altered the subcellular distribution of N-ras (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gal-1 is not known to impact on N-ras nanoclustering.
source: Gal-1 is not known to impact on N-ras nanoclustering and binding to it remained unaltered by the mutations in N-ras (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Binding of N-ras mutants to Gal-1 remained unaltered.
source: Gal-1 is not known to impact on N-ras nanoclustering and binding to it remained unaltered by the mutations in N-ras (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Gal-1-complexation FRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation T50I in N-ras had no significant effect on nanoclustering.
source: While mutation T50I had no significant effect, both mutation E49K and C51Y significantly increased nanoclustering (Figure 5B,C)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and FRET data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Mutations E49K and C51Y in N-ras significantly increased nanoclustering.
source: While mutation T50I had no significant effect, both mutation E49K and C51Y significantly increased nanoclustering (Figure 5B,C)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and FRET data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Mutations E49K and C51Y in N-ras significantly increased Ras effector recruitment compared to parent N-rasG12V.
source: While mutation T50I had no significant effect, both mutation E49K and C51Y significantly increased nanoclustering (Figure 5B,C) and ensuing Ras effector recruitment as compared to parent N-rasG12V (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: All N-ras mutants bound the RBD indistinguishably from N-ras without switch III mutations.
source: All mutants bound the RBD indistinguishably from N-ras without switch III mutations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by compactin-treatment RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: N-ras-E49K, N-ras-C51Y, and N-ras-T50I remained sensitive to GAP-mediated hydrolysis.
source: Moreover, both hyperactive mutants N-ras-E49K and N-ras-C51Y, as well as N-ras-T50I remained sensitive to GAP-mediated hydrolysis and did not display increased background activation of MEK, ERK, or AKT in the absence of serum (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown and Western blot data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: N-ras-E49K, N-ras-C51Y, and N-ras-T50I did not display increased background activation of MEK, ERK, or AKT in the absence of serum.
source: Moreover, both hyperactive mutants N-ras-E49K and N-ras-C51Y, as well as N-ras-T50I remained sensitive to GAP-mediated hydrolysis and did not display increased background activation of MEK, ERK, or AKT in the absence of serum (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Increased RBD-recruitment of N-ras-E49K and N-ras-C51Y followed augmented nanoclustering.
source: Thus, basic biochemical parameters were largely preserved, confirming that increased RBD-recruitment followed augmented nanoclustering of N-ras with switch III mutations E49K or C51Y.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: RASopathy-associated Ras mutants do not lead to a clear increase of the downstream pathway.
source: It was previously observed that RASopathy-associated Ras mutants do not lead to a clear increase of the downstream pathway (Gremer et al., 2011; Cirstea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neither GTP-loading nor phosphorylation of MEK, ERK, and AKT was clearly increased after EGF-stimulation for N-ras switch III mutants.
source: Similar to these observations, neither GTP-loading (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) nor phosphorylation of MEK, ERK, and AKT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) was clearly increased after EGF-stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown and Western blot data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: PC12 cells transfected with N-rasG12V-E49K or N-rasG12V-C51Y showed significantly increased neurite length.
source: PC12 cells transfected with mGFP-tagged mutant N-rasG12V-E49K or N-rasG12V-C51Y showed significantly increased neurite length (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by PC12 differentiation assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing N-rasG12V-C51Y showed significantly increased cell proliferation.
source: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing this mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) showed significantly increased cell proliferation (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing N-rasG12V-C51Y showed significantly increased focus formation.
source: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing this mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) showed significantly increased cell proliferation (Figure 5G), focus formation (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by focus formation assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing N-rasG12V-C51Y showed significantly increased anchorage-independent growth in soft agar.
source: NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing this mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) showed significantly increased cell proliferation (Figure 5G), focus formation (Figure 5H), and anchorage-independent growth in soft agar (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Cancer-derived mutations E49K and C51Y do not affect relevant biochemical functions of N-ras.
source: In summary, cancer-derived mutations E49K and C51Y do not affect relevant biochemical functions of N-ras, but instead increase its nanoclustering potential to enhance effector recruitment and subsequent Ras/MAPK-signaling output.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Cancer-derived mutations E49K and C51Y increase N-ras nanoclustering potential to enhance effector recruitment and subsequent Ras/MAPK-signaling output.
source: In summary, cancer-derived mutations E49K and C51Y do not affect relevant biochemical functions of N-ras, but instead increase its nanoclustering potential to enhance effector recruitment and subsequent Ras/MAPK-signaling output.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: N-rasG12V-C51Y increases cell proliferation and tumorigenic growth of transformed cells.
source: Our most active N-ras mutant furthermore revealed that augmented nanoclustering ultimately increases cell proliferation and tumorigenic growth of transformed cells.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation, transformation, and soft agar assay data.

claim: KRAS is the developmentally most significant Ras isoform.
source: The KRAS gene is the developmentally most significant Ras isoform.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS.

claim: Activating germline mutations associated with the K-ras4B isoform lead to relatively severe RASopathy phenotypes.
source: Its important developmental role is furthermore underscored by the fact that activating germline mutations that are associated with the K-ras4B isoform (henceforth K-ras) lead to relatively severe RASopathy phenotypes (Carta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: K-ras-V152G is a Noonan syndrome-associated mutation on helix α5 of the switch III.
source: In addition to our N-rasT50I mutant, we therefore added the Noonan syndrome-associated mutation V152G on helix α5 of the switch III of K-ras to our otherwise cancer mutation-focused analysis.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of RASopathy mutations.

claim: K-ras-V152G and N-ras-T50I represent mechanistically unresolved switch III mutations in RASopathies.
source: These two mutations represented mechanistically unresolved switch III mutations in RASopathies.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Subcellular distribution of K-ras-V152G remained unchanged.
source: Like for the N-ras Noonan syndrome mutant, subcellular distribution remained unchanged (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: K-ras-V152G showed no increase in nanoclustering.
source: Like for the N-ras Noonan syndrome mutant, subcellular distribution remained unchanged (Figure 6A) and no increase in nanoclustering (Figure 6B,C)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and FRET data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: K-ras-V152G showed no increase in effector recruitment.
source: Like for the N-ras Noonan syndrome mutant, subcellular distribution remained unchanged (Figure 6A) and no increase in nanoclustering (Figure 6B,C), effector recruitment (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: K-ras-V152G showed no increase in PC12 differentiation.
source: Like for the N-ras Noonan syndrome mutant, subcellular distribution remained unchanged (Figure 6A) and no increase in nanoclustering (Figure 6B,C), effector recruitment (Figure 6D) or PC12 differentiation (Figure 6F) was found.
evidence: This is supported by PC12 differentiation assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The binding of K-ras-V152G to the RBD in solution was unchanged compared to the parent K-ras.
source: Also the binding of the mutant to the RBD in solution was unchanged compared to the parent K-ras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by compactin-treatment RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: K-ras-V152G GAP sensitivity was unaltered.
source: Also the binding of the mutant to the RBD in solution was unchanged compared to the parent K-ras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and its GAP sensitivity and downstream signaling activity under serum starvation were unaltered (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown and Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: K-ras-V152G downstream signaling activity under serum starvation was unaltered.
source: Also the binding of the mutant to the RBD in solution was unchanged compared to the parent K-ras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), and its GAP sensitivity and downstream signaling activity under serum starvation were unaltered (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The R164Q mutation in K-ras was found in colorectal and endometrial cancers.
source: We then turned to investigate the most frequent switch III mutation, R164Q in K-ras, which was found in colorectal and endometrial cancers.
evidence: This is based on cancer genomic database analysis.

claim: K-ras-R164Q alone (in the wt background) did not possess any detectable increase in its transforming potential.
source: A previous study by others showed that this helix α5 mutation alone (i.e., in the wt background) did not possess any detectable increase in its transforming potential, yet gene expression analysis suggested a mild activation phenotype (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Gene expression analysis of K-ras-R164Q suggested a mild activation phenotype.
source: A previous study by others showed that this helix α5 mutation alone (i.e., in the wt background) did not possess any detectable increase in its transforming potential, yet gene expression analysis suggested a mild activation phenotype (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Addition of R164Q did not alter the subcellular distribution of K-rasG12V in BHK cells.
source: Addition of R164Q did not alter the subcellular distribution of mGFP-tagged K-rasG12V (Figure 6A) in BHK cells.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Binding of K-ras mutants to Gal-1 was unaltered.
source: Like for the N-ras mutants, binding to Gal-1 was unaltered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by Gal-1-complexation FRET data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nanoclustering of K-rasG12V-R164Q was significantly increased compared to the parent K-ras.
source: Nanoclustering analysis of K-rasG12V-R164Q by electron microscopic- (Figure 6B) and by nanoclustering-FRET-analysis (Figure 6C) in BHK cells both confirmed significantly increased nanoclustering as compared to the parent K-ras.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and FRET data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Augmented nanoclustering of K-rasG12V-R164Q was strictly followed by increased recruitment of the effector fragment RBD in BHK cells.
source: In agreement with our nanocluster-activity model (Figure 1A), augmented nanoclustering was strictly followed by an increased recruitment of the effector fragment RBD in BHK cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The effector fragment was bound equally to K-ras-R164Q and to the parent K-ras in solution.
source: Importantly, in solution the effector fragment again was bound equally to the mutant and to the parent K-ras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by compactin-treatment RBD-recruitment FRET data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: K-ras-R164Q is sensitive to GAP-mediated inactivation.
source: Together with the normal GAP-sensitivity of K-ras-R164Q (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), these results support that the mutation neither affected the affinity to the RBD of C-Raf nor GAP-mediated Ras inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by RBD-pulldown data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The R164Q mutation neither affected the affinity to the RBD of C-Raf nor GAP-mediated Ras inactivation.
source: Together with the normal GAP-sensitivity of K-ras-R164Q (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), these results support that the mutation neither affected the affinity to the RBD of C-Raf nor GAP-mediated Ras inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: K-rasG12V-R164Q showed increased Ras/MAPK activity by significantly increased PC12 cell differentiation.
source: As for the two N-ras nanocluster mutations, we observed increased Ras/MAPK activity of K-rasG12V-R164Q by significantly increased PC12 cell differentiation (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by PC12 differentiation assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: K-rasG12V-R164Q did not show increased Ras/MAPK activity on the phospho-protein level.
source: As for the two N-ras nanocluster mutations, we observed increased Ras/MAPK activity of K-rasG12V-R164Q by significantly increased PC12 cell differentiation (Figure 6F) but not on the phospho-protein level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells expressing K-rasG12V-R164Q proliferated faster than K-rasG12V parent.
source: In agreement with this hyperactivation phenotype, NIH/3T3 cells expressing the mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) proliferated faster (Figure 6G)
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells expressing K-rasG12V-R164Q were more transformed than the K-rasG12V parent.
source: In agreement with this hyperactivation phenotype, NIH/3T3 cells expressing the mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) proliferated faster (Figure 6G), were more transformed (Figure 6H)
evidence: This is supported by focus formation assay data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells expressing K-rasG12V-R164Q grew more anchorage independently in soft agar than the K-rasG12V parent.
source: In agreement with this hyperactivation phenotype, NIH/3T3 cells expressing the mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) proliferated faster (Figure 6G), were more transformed (Figure 6H), and grew more anchorage independently in soft agar (Figure 6I) than the K-rasG12V parent.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Mutation R164Q in K-ras increases cell proliferation and tumorigenicity by its increased nanoclustering.
source: Thus mutation R164Q in K-ras increases cell proliferation and tumorigenicity by its increased nanoclustering.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Rare cancer-associated mutations in the switch III regions of H-, N-, and K-ras can increase effector engagement while not changing the affinity to the effector.
source: Here, we have described an unprecedented mechanism for the activation of a signaling protein in cancer. We showed that rare cancer-associated mutations in the switch III regions of H-, N-, and K-ras can increase effector engagement, while not changing the affinity to the effector.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data.

claim: The increase of the nanoscale concentration of Ras in nanocluster hyperactivates Ras to promote tumorigenic growth.
source: Instead the increase of the nanoscale concentration of Ras in nanocluster hyperactivates Ras to promote tumorigenic growth (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 7.
